problem: Existing vision-and-language work recognizes objects or describes images in a single observational sentence, but does not infer why objects are present or narrate what happened or might happen; commonsense affordance knowledge is not systematically available for reuse.
motivation: A robot navigating an environment and collecting images needs to explain what happens, or might have happened, in a scene to support human-robot interaction. This requires commonsense reasoning beyond visual cues and narrative generation beyond single-sentence captions, both of which are missing from current VQA and captioning resources.
key_idea: Combine bottom-up commonsense reasoning from qualia relations encoded in the Rich Event Ontology (to infer scene function from objects) with top-down narratological schema and crowd-sourced narrative elements to generate narratives about robot-collected images.
insight: The paper is a position/short proposal with no experiments or ablations. Its argument is that object qualia (used_for, functions_as, is_a) chained with event roles can infer scene type (e.g., pot and cereal lead to kitchen). Human pilot narratives already show extrapolation and causal reasoning beyond what is depicted, which single-sentence captioning cannot capture.
method: Qualia-based visual understanding: query recognized objects for qualia relations (Agentive, Telic, Constitutive, Formal) in the Rich Event Ontology to get affordances (e.g., pot used_for cooking)
Location inference via REO semantic roles: map activities and object classes (cooking Prepared_Food) to common locations (kitchen) to infer that the space functions_as a kitchen
Framing/content selection: use a few open-ended prompts (e.g., what happened) to elicit narratives that go beyond the observable
Narrative generation: apply existing narratological schema and elements top-down, using crowd-sourced narrative elements as content
Resources: crowdsourced annotations and the ontology to be released to the community

setting.backbone: none (conceptual proposal; assumes an object recognizer plus the REO ontology)
setting.training_data: none; pilot human-authored narratives (Lukin et al. 2018) and crowdsourced qualia annotations
setting.observation: images taken onboard a robot during human-robot interaction
setting.privileged: assumes objects in the image are recognized accurately

numbers_note: No experiments or results reported; short position paper.
results: No quantitative results. Preliminary qualitative analysis of human-authored narratives about a robot-captured office image shows extrapolation beyond the visible and creative causal reasoning.
limitations: No implementation or quantitative evaluation; approach is a sketch with ongoing work
Assumes accurate object recognition and a still-incomplete set of qualia relations
Not a navigation method; relevance to embodied navigation is only via robot-collected images and narration
builds_on: Lukin et al. 2018 pipeline narrative data collection
